title: Al Capone, 1931 — the gangster brought down by his taxes
sources: Wikipedia: Al Capone — boss of the Chicago Outfit during Prohibition; widely assumed responsible for ordering the 1929 Saint Valentine's Day Massacre, despite being at his Florida home at the time; in 1927 the Supreme Court ruled in United States v. Sullivan that illegally earned income was subject to income tax; the key to his conviction was proving his income, and the most valuable evidence came from his own offer to pay tax — his lawyer admitted income for various years; his defence claimed his income was lost to gambling; the judge allowed his spending to be presented at very great length; convicted on five counts of income tax evasion on 17 October 1931 and sentenced to 11 years in federal prison; at Alcatraz he played banjo in the prison band, the Rock Islanders; he sponsored a soup kitchen in Chicago during the Depression
Wikipedia: Frank J. Wilson — in the fall of 1930 he discovered a ledger of a large gambling operation, with net income divided among individuals referred to as A, R and J
Also on this day (candidates.md, in the app): 1814 the London Beer Flood; 1777 Burgoyne surrenders at Saratoga

post.facebook:
On this day in 1931, Al Capone — boss of Chicago's bootlegging empire — was convicted. Not of murder, but of income tax evasion.

He was widely blamed for the 1929 Saint Valentine's Day Massacre, but he was at his Florida home that day. So federal authorities went after his money. In 1927 the Supreme Court had ruled that even illegal income was subject to tax.

Treasury agent Frank Wilson found a ledger from a huge gambling operation, with profits divided among people called only "A", "R" and "J". But the most valuable evidence came from Capone himself: trying to settle with the government, his lawyer had already admitted his income. In court, the defence claimed he had lost it all gambling — while the court heard, at great length, about his spending.

Guilty on five counts. Eleven years in federal prison. At Alcatraz, the former boss of Chicago played banjo in the prison band.

Also on 17 October: the London Beer Flood (1814), and Burgoyne's surrender at Saratoga (1777).

youtube.description:
17 October 1931: Al Capone, boss of Chicago's bootlegging empire, was convicted — not of murder, but of income tax evasion. Blamed for the Saint Valentine's Day Massacre while he was in Florida, he was finally caught by his money: a Supreme Court ruling that illegal income is taxable, a ledger paying profits to someone called "A", and his own lawyer's admission of his income. His defence said he'd lost it all gambling. Guilty on five counts, eleven years — and at Alcatraz, he played banjo in the prison band.

Also on 17 October: the London Beer Flood (1814) and the surrender at Saratoga (1777).
